name: 3. System design and architecture
description: Stack, components, data flow, hosting, scaling, API style.

cards.subject: A monolith
says: deploys all application code as a single unit
shares one process and usually one database across all features
cards.use: want the simplest deployment for a small team
not: cannot have any internal structure

cards.subject: Microservices
says: splits a system into independently deployable services
lets each service own its own data store
replaces in-process calls with network calls
cards.use: need separate teams to release and scale parts independently
not: removes the need to handle partial failure

cards.subject: Layered architecture
says: separates presentation, business logic and data access into tiers
restricts each layer to calling the layer below it
cards.use: want a familiar separation of concerns inside one application
not: requires each layer to run on its own server

cards.subject: A modular monolith
says: keeps one deployable unit with strict module boundaries
allows modules to be split into services later if needed
cards.use: want clear boundaries without the operational cost of distribution
not: needs a network call between every pair of modules

cards.subject: Hexagonal architecture
says: isolates the domain from infrastructure behind ports and adapters
lets a database or UI be swapped without changing core logic
cards.use: want to test business rules without a database or web server
not: places the database at the centre of the design

cards.subject: Event-driven architecture
says: has components communicate by publishing and reacting to events
keeps producers unaware of who consumes their events
cards.use: need several systems to react to something that happened without direct calls
not: requires each caller to wait for a reply

cards.subject: Serverless architecture
says: runs code as functions managed by the platform
bills by usage and can scale to zero when idle
cards.use: have spiky or infrequent workloads and no wish to manage servers
not: runs without any servers at all

cards.subject: CQRS
says: separates the model that changes data from the model that reads it
lets read models be shaped and scaled independently of writes
cards.use: need reads and writes with very different shapes or load
not: requires event sourcing

cards.subject: Event sourcing
says: stores state as an append-only sequence of events
rebuilds current state by replaying events
cards.use: need a full audit trail and the ability to reconstruct past state
not: keeps only the latest row for each entity

cards.subject: Availability
says: measures the proportion of time a system can serve requests
is commonly stated as a percentage of uptime
cards.use: need to state how much downtime is acceptable
not: measures how fast one request completes

cards.subject: Reliability
says: measures how consistently a system produces correct results over time
covers correct behaviour, not just being reachable

cards.subject: Scalability
says: describes how well a system copes with growing load by adding resources
is judged by how cost and performance change as load grows
cards.use: expect usage to grow many times over
not: means the system is fast under today's load

cards.subject: Latency
says: measures the time taken to complete one request
is usually reported as percentiles such as p99
cards.use: need to know how long a user waits for a response
not: counts requests completed per second

cards.subject: Throughput
says: measures how many requests or units of work complete per unit of time
cards.use: need to know how much work a system can process in total
not: measures the delay of a single request

cards.subject: Maintainability
says: describes how easily a system can be understood, changed and fixed
cards.use: see changes taking longer and breaking unrelated things

cards.subject: Testability
says: describes how easily behaviour can be verified in isolation
improves when dependencies can be replaced with test doubles
cards.use: find a component can only be tested with the whole system running

cards.subject: Observability
says: lets you infer internal state from logs, metrics and traces
helps explain failures nobody predicted
cards.use: must find out why a rare production failure happened
not: is the same as having a dashboard of known alerts

cards.subject: Elasticity
says: adds and removes capacity automatically as demand changes
avoids paying for idle capacity at quiet times
cards.use: face demand that rises sharply for a day and then falls

cards.subject: Recovery time objective
says: states the longest acceptable time to restore service after an outage
cards.use: need to agree how quickly service must return after a disaster
not: states how much data may be lost

cards.subject: Recovery point objective
says: states the longest acceptable window of data loss measured in time
drives how often backups or replication must run
cards.use: need to agree how much recent data can be lost in a failure
not: states how fast service must return

cards.subject: An architecture decision record
says: captures one significant decision with its context and consequences
is stored with the code and rarely edited once accepted
cards.use: want future engineers to know why a choice was made
not: records every code change

cards.subject: The C4 system context diagram
says: shows the system as one box among its users and external systems
leaves out internal technology detail
cards.use: need to explain the system to a non-technical audience

cards.subject: The C4 container diagram
says: shows separately runnable parts such as web apps, APIs and databases
labels the technology and protocol between those parts
cards.use: need to show which deployable pieces exist and how they talk

cards.subject: The C4 component diagram
says: shows the major building blocks inside a single container
cards.use: need to explain how one service is organised internally

cards.subject: A sequence diagram
says: shows messages between participants in time order
suits explaining one request flow end to end
cards.use: need to show who calls whom, and in what order, for a single scenario
not: shows the static structure of every component

cards.subject: A design document
says: proposes a solution to a specific problem before it is built
lists alternatives considered and why they were rejected
cards.use: need to review an approach with peers before writing the code
not: is written only after release

cards.subject: A non-functional requirement
says: states how well a system must perform rather than what it does
covers targets such as response time, availability and security
cards.use: must specify response time or availability targets
not: describes a user-visible feature

cards.subject: A quality attribute scenario
says: specifies a stimulus, environment and measurable response
turns a vague wish such as be fast into a testable statement
cards.use: hear a stakeholder ask for a system that is fast or secure
not: is a user story for a new feature

cards.subject: ATAM
says: evaluates an architecture against quality attribute scenarios
exposes trade-off points, sensitivity points and risks
cards.use: need a structured review of whether an architecture meets competing quality goals
not: is a load-testing tool

cards.subject: A message queue
says: holds messages until a consumer processes them
delivers each message to one consumer in a competing group
cards.use: need to hand work off for asynchronous processing
not: delivers every message to all consumers

cards.subject: Publish-subscribe
says: delivers a copy of each message to every subscriber
keeps publishers unaware of their subscribers
cards.use: need several services to each react to the same event
not: gives each message to a single consumer only

cards.subject: An API gateway
says: provides a single entry point that routes requests to backend services
centralises edge concerns such as authentication and rate limiting
cards.use: want clients to call one address instead of many services

cards.subject: A backend for frontend
says: provides a separate API tailored to each client type
cards.use: need mobile and web clients to receive differently shaped responses
not: is a single shared API for all client types

cards.subject: A dead letter queue
says: collects messages that repeatedly fail processing
lets failures be inspected without blocking the main queue
cards.use: find one poison message keeps blocking a consumer

cards.subject: An idempotency key
says: lets a repeated request be recognised and applied only once
is sent by the client with a request that may be retried
cards.use: need to retry payment-style requests without double effects

cards.subject: A webhook
says: lets a server call a client URL when an event occurs
avoids the client polling for changes
cards.use: want to be told when something happens instead of asking repeatedly

cards.subject: The transactional outbox
says: writes an event to a table in the same database transaction as the data change
lets a separate relay publish the event afterwards
cards.use: must not lose or invent events when updating a database and publishing a message
not: publishes the message before the database commit

cards.subject: A saga
says: coordinates a multi-service business transaction as local transactions
undoes earlier steps with compensating actions when a later one fails
cards.use: need an order flow across payment, stock and shipping services without a distributed lock
not: holds one database lock across all services

cards.subject: An anti-corruption layer
says: translates between a legacy model and a new domain model
stops legacy concepts leaking into new code
cards.use: must integrate a new service with a legacy system whose model is messy

cards.subject: The strangler fig pattern
says: replaces a legacy system gradually by routing slices of traffic to new code
lets old and new run side by side until the old is retired
cards.use: need to migrate a large legacy system without a big-bang rewrite
not: requires freezing all features during a rewrite

cards.subject: Horizontal scaling
says: adds more machines or instances to share the load
needs the service to be stateless or to keep its state outside the instance
cards.use: want to add capacity by running more copies
not: adds more CPU and memory to one machine

cards.subject: Vertical scaling
says: adds more CPU or memory to an existing machine
hits a hardware ceiling and keeps a single point of failure
cards.use: want a quick capacity boost without changing the application
not: adds more instances behind a load balancer

cards.subject: A load balancer
says: spreads incoming requests across several instances
removes failed instances from rotation using health checks
cards.use: need requests shared across several identical servers

cards.subject: A content delivery network
says: serves static content from locations near users
reduces load on the origin server
cards.use: want images and scripts delivered quickly worldwide

cards.subject: The cache-aside pattern
says: has the application check the cache first and load from the database on a miss
fills the cache only with data that was actually requested
cards.use: want a simple cache where the application controls what is stored
not: writes to the cache and database together on every update

cards.subject: A write-through cache
says: writes to the cache and the underlying store together on each update
keeps cache and store consistent at the cost of slower writes
cards.use: need reads always to find fresh data in the cache
not: acknowledges a write before it reaches the store

cards.subject: Cache invalidation
says: removes or refreshes cached data when the source changes
is hard because stale reads can persist if an update is missed
cards.use: see users getting out-of-date data after an update

cards.subject: A read replica
says: serves read queries from a copy of the primary database
can return slightly stale data because of replication lag
cards.use: have a read-heavy workload on a single database
not: accepts writes independently of the primary

cards.subject: Sharding
says: splits data across databases by a key
makes queries that span shards harder
cards.use: have more data or write load than one database server can handle
not: copies the same data to every server

cards.subject: Back pressure
says: slows or rejects incoming work when a consumer cannot keep up
prevents unbounded queues
cards.use: find a fast producer keeps overwhelming a slow consumer

cards.subject: Rate limiting
says: caps the number of requests a client may make in a period
protects a service from abuse and overload
cards.use: need to stop one client using all the capacity

cards.subject: A cache stampede
says: happens when many requests miss an expired entry at once and hit the origin
is reduced by request coalescing or staggered expiry
cards.use: see the database fall over whenever a popular cache entry expires
not: happens when the cache is too small to hold anything

cards.subject: A hot key
says: overloads one shard because traffic concentrates on a single key
is not fixed by adding more shards alone
cards.use: see one shard saturated while the others sit idle

cards.subject: ACID
says: guarantees atomic, consistent, isolated and durable transactions
is the traditional transaction model of relational databases
cards.use: need a multi-row update to either fully happen or not at all

cards.subject: Eventual consistency
says: lets replicas differ temporarily but converge once updates stop
accepts that a read may return stale data for a while
cards.use: can tolerate briefly stale reads in return for availability
not: guarantees every read sees the latest write

cards.subject: Strong consistency
says: ensures a read returns the most recent completed write
costs latency or availability across replicas
cards.use: must never show a user an outdated account balance

cards.subject: The CAP theorem
says: states that during a network partition a system must choose between consistency and availability
applies to the behaviour of a distributed system when a partition occurs
cards.use: need to explain what a distributed store gives up during a network split
not: lets a system keep all three guarantees during a partition

cards.subject: Two-phase commit
says: has a coordinator ask all participants to prepare and then commit
can block participants if the coordinator fails
cards.use: need an atomic commit across several databases

cards.subject: Optimistic locking
says: detects conflicting updates with a version check at write time
fits data that is rarely updated by two users at once
cards.use: expect conflicts to be rare and want to avoid holding locks
not: locks the record for the whole time a user edits it

cards.subject: Pessimistic locking
says: locks a record while one transaction works on it
reduces concurrency but suits high-contention data
cards.use: expect frequent competing updates to the same row
not: only checks for conflicts when the write happens

cards.subject: A quorum
says: requires a majority of replicas to agree on a read or write
lets a system tolerate the failure of a minority of nodes
cards.use: need replicated writes to survive node failures while staying consistent

cards.subject: Split brain
says: happens when partitioned nodes each believe they are the leader
is prevented by requiring a quorum to elect a leader
cards.use: see two nodes accepting conflicting writes after a network partition

cards.subject: A timeout
says: bounds how long a caller waits for a response
stops a slow dependency from holding resources forever
cards.use: want a caller to give up instead of waiting indefinitely
not: makes the slow dependency faster

cards.subject: Retry with exponential backoff
says: repeats a failed call after increasing delays
avoids hammering a recovering service
cards.use: face brief, transient failures when calling a dependency
not: retries immediately in a tight loop

cards.subject: Jitter
says: adds randomness to retry delays
stops many clients retrying at the same instant
cards.use: see clients that failed together all retry together

cards.subject: A circuit breaker
says: stops calls to a failing dependency after repeated errors
probes now and then to see if the dependency has recovered
cards.use: want to fail fast when a downstream service is clearly down
not: retries every failed call indefinitely

cards.subject: A bulkhead
says: isolates resources such as thread pools per dependency
stops one failing dependency from exhausting capacity for everything
cards.use: find one slow dependency can starve unrelated features of threads

cards.subject: Load shedding
says: drops low-priority work when overloaded to protect core functions
rejects excess requests rather than letting all of them time out
cards.use: face overload and want the critical requests to keep succeeding

cards.subject: A health check
says: lets a load balancer or orchestrator test whether an instance is working
cards.use: need unhealthy instances to be taken out of rotation automatically

cards.subject: Graceful degradation
says: keeps core features working while non-essential ones are switched off
cards.use: want checkout to keep working when recommendations are down

cards.subject: Chaos engineering
says: injects controlled failures to test how a system copes
is run to find weaknesses before real outages do
cards.use: want evidence that failover really works before a real outage

cards.subject: A retry storm
says: happens when many clients retry a failing service and multiply its load
can turn a brief fault into a prolonged outage
cards.use: see a recovering service knocked over again by returning clients

cards.subject: REST
says: models resources identified by URLs and handled with HTTP verbs
keeps each request independent so servers hold no client session state
cards.use: want a widely understood API built on plain HTTP

cards.subject: GraphQL
says: lets the client request exactly the fields it needs from a single endpoint
can allow very expensive queries unless depth or cost is limited
cards.use: have clients that need differently shaped data from the same backend

cards.subject: gRPC
says: uses Protocol Buffers over HTTP/2 for typed service-to-service calls
supports streaming in both directions
cards.use: need efficient, strongly typed calls between internal services

cards.subject: OpenAPI
says: describes a REST API in a machine-readable specification
is used to generate documentation and client code
cards.use: want documentation and client libraries generated from one API contract

cards.subject: Cursor pagination
says: returns a token pointing to the last item seen
stays stable when rows are inserted while paging
cards.use: page through a feed that changes while users scroll
not: jumps to a page by skipping a number of rows

cards.subject: Offset pagination
says: skips a number of rows and returns the next page
can repeat or miss items when data changes between requests
not: stays stable under concurrent inserts

cards.subject: API versioning
says: lets a breaking change be released without breaking existing clients
runs old and new contract versions side by side for a time
cards.use: must make a breaking change to a public API

cards.subject: An idempotent HTTP method
says: can be repeated with the same effect as a single call
includes PUT and DELETE
cards.use: want a client to be able to retry a request safely
not: is the same thing as a safe method

cards.subject: The 429 status code
says: tells a client it has sent too many requests
is often accompanied by a Retry-After header
cards.use: must tell a client to slow down

cards.subject: An additive change
says: adds optional fields or endpoints without breaking existing consumers
is the safe default for evolving a public API
cards.use: need to extend an API without forcing every client to update
not: removes a field that clients still read

cards.subject: Infrastructure as code
says: defines servers and networks in version-controlled files
makes environments reproducible and reviewable
cards.use: want the same environment recreated reliably and changes reviewed
not: relies on engineers clicking through a console

cards.subject: IaaS
says: rents virtual machines, storage and networks
leaves operating system patching to the customer

cards.subject: PaaS
says: runs customer code on a managed platform
hides operating system management from the customer
cards.use: want to deploy code without managing servers' operating systems

cards.subject: A container
says: packages an application with its dependencies and shares the host kernel
starts faster than a full virtual machine
cards.use: need the same package to run identically on a laptop and a server
not: includes a complete guest operating system kernel

cards.subject: Kubernetes
says: orchestrates containers across a cluster
restarts failed containers and keeps replicas at a declared desired state
cards.use: need to run and heal many containers across many machines

cards.subject: An availability zone
says: is an isolated location within a cloud region
lets a service survive a data centre failure when spread across several
cards.use: want a service to survive the loss of one data centre

cards.subject: Blue-green deployment
says: keeps two identical environments and switches traffic between them
allows instant rollback by switching traffic back
cards.use: need to roll back a release within minutes
not: sends a small percentage of traffic to the new version first

cards.subject: A canary release
says: sends a small share of traffic to the new version first
limits the blast radius of a bad release
cards.use: want a risky change tried on a few users before everyone
not: switches all traffic at once

cards.subject: A feature flag
says: decouples deploying code from releasing a feature
lets a feature be switched off without a redeploy
cards.use: want to ship code dark and turn it on later

cards.subject: The twelve-factor app
says: keeps configuration in the environment instead of in code
treats logs as event streams and processes as stateless
cards.use: want an application that is portable and easy to scale out

cards.subject: A multi-region deployment
says: runs in more than one region for disaster recovery or latency
adds data replication and consistency complexity
cards.use: must survive the loss of an entire region
not: is achieved simply by adding availability zones

cards.subject: Least privilege
says: grants only the access needed for the task
limits the damage a compromised account can do
cards.use: are setting permissions for a service account

cards.subject: Defence in depth
says: layers several independent controls so one failure is not fatal
cards.use: want no single control failure to expose the system
not: relies on one strong perimeter

cards.subject: Secure by default
says: ships with the safest configuration so insecurity needs an explicit choice

cards.subject: Attack surface
says: is the sum of points where an attacker can try to enter or extract data
shrinks when unused features and ports are removed
cards.use: want to reduce the ways a system can be attacked

cards.subject: Zero trust
says: does not trust a request just because it comes from inside the network
verifies identity and authorisation on every request
cards.use: cannot rely on the office network as a security boundary
not: trusts everything inside the firewall

cards.subject: Threat modelling
says: identifies what could go wrong with a design before it is built
asks what we are building, what can go wrong and what we will do about it
cards.use: want to find design flaws before writing code

cards.subject: Fail closed
says: denies access when a security check cannot be completed
cards.use: want an outage of the auth service not to open the door
not: allows access when the check is unavailable

cards.subject: Secrets management
says: stores credentials in a dedicated store instead of code or images
supports rotation and audit
cards.use: find credentials committed in a repository

cards.subject: STRIDE
says: categorises threats as spoofing, tampering, repudiation, disclosure, denial of service and elevation of privilege
cards.use: want a checklist of threat categories for a threat model

cards.subject: A trust boundary
says: marks where data moves between components with different trust levels
is where validation and authentication checks belong
cards.use: need to decide where to validate untrusted input

cards.subject: A fitness function
says: automatically checks that an architectural characteristic is preserved
runs in the build pipeline to guard against drift
cards.use: want an architecture rule enforced automatically rather than by review

cards.subject: Conway's law
says: observes that system design mirrors the communication structure of the organisation
is applied in reverse by shaping teams to get the desired architecture
cards.use: find service boundaries always follow the org chart

cards.subject: A bounded context
says: defines the boundary within which a domain model and its terms are consistent
lets the same word mean different things in different contexts
cards.use: find one shared model is forcing every team into the same definitions

cards.subject: Coupling
says: measures how much one component depends on another
is reduced by depending on interfaces instead of implementations

cards.subject: Cohesion
says: measures how closely the responsibilities inside a module belong together

cards.subject: Technical debt
says: is the future cost incurred by choosing a quick solution now
grows interest in the form of slower changes if left unpaid
cards.use: must explain why shortcuts make later work slower

cards.subject: Domain-driven design
says: models software around the business domain using a shared language
cards.use: find developers and domain experts misunderstand each other

cards.subject: Dependency inversion
says: makes high-level code depend on abstractions rather than concrete details
cards.use: want business logic not to depend on a specific database library

cards.subject: A walking skeleton
says: is a thin end-to-end implementation of the main components
proves the architecture early by running through every layer
cards.use: want to prove the main parts connect before building features

cards.subject: A reversible decision
says: can be undone cheaply so it can be made quickly
needs less analysis than a hard-to-reverse one
cards.use: are deciding how much deliberation a choice deserves

cards.subject: A distributed monolith
says: has services that must be deployed together because of tight coupling
combines microservice network costs with monolith coupling
cards.use: find every release needs five services deployed in lockstep

cards.subject: A big ball of mud
says: has no discernible structure, with everything depending on everything

cards.subject: The golden hammer
says: applies a favourite tool to every problem whether it fits or not

cards.subject: Premature optimisation
says: tunes performance before measuring where the bottleneck is
cards.use: are tempted to rewrite code for speed with no profiling data

cards.subject: A single point of failure
says: is one component whose failure stops the whole system

cards.subject: Shared-database integration
says: couples services through the same tables so a schema change breaks several
bypasses any service API as the contract between services
cards.use: find a column rename in one service broke another

cards.subject: A cascading failure
says: spreads from one failing component to the components that depend on it
cards.use: see one slow service bring down callers several hops away

cards.subject: Resume-driven design
says: picks technology for career benefit rather than project fit

cards.subject: The gglearn stack
says: uses Next.js with SQLite through Drizzle
is run by PM2 on a server behind Cloudflare
cards.use: need to know what gglearn is built on
not: uses plain PHP with MySQL

cards.subject: The ggmoney stack
says: is plain PHP 8.1 or newer with no Composer packages
uses SQLite by default and MySQL on the live server
cards.use: need to know what ggmoney is built on
not: is built on Next.js

cards.subject: The ggmoney per-driver schema
says: keeps one schema per database driver instead of translating at runtime
accepts some duplication to avoid silent translation bugs in a finance app
cards.use: wonder why a finance app duplicates schema files
not: is generated at runtime from a single schema

cards.subject: The gglearn request path
says: runs from the visitor through Cloudflare and Apache to the PM2 app
has Apache terminate TLS through certbot and reverse-proxy to the app
cards.use: need to trace a production request for logging or debugging
not: lets visitors reach the app directly on a public port

cards.subject: The gglearn-web app
says: is a PM2 process listening on 127.0.0.1 port 3400
is not exposed directly to the internet
cards.use: wonder why the app cannot be reached directly from outside the server

cards.subject: The X-Forwarded-For hop rule
says: picks the client address a fixed number of hops from the end of the header, defaulting to two
ignores whatever a visitor puts at the start of the header
cards.use: need to know how the rate limiter finds the real client address
not: trusts the first address in the header

cards.subject: The Apache Cloudflare snippet
says: can restrict access to Cloudflare ranges so the proxy cannot be bypassed
takes effect only once the live virtual hosts include it
cards.use: worry that someone reaching Apache directly could spoof the client address

cards.subject: The gglearn deploy script
says: syncs files with rsync while excluding node_modules, build output, databases and environment files
takes a flock lock so two deploys cannot run at once
runs npm ci for repeatable installs
cards.use: need to know what the deploy script does before touching the server

cards.subject: The deploy schema push
says: runs drizzle-kit with no force flag
stops the deploy instead of deleting rows when a change is destructive
cards.use: worry that a deploy could silently delete data
not: forces destructive changes through automatically

cards.subject: The deploy health check
says: requires the app to answer HTTP 200 several times
fails the deploy and shows PM2 error logs if it does not
cards.use: want to know how the deploy verifies the app came up

cards.subject: The gglearn GitHub Actions workflow
says: runs the deploy script on every push to main
cards.use: wonder what triggers a production deploy

cards.subject: The gglearn rate limiter
says: keeps its counters in process memory
must move its counters to the database if the process count changes
cards.use: plan to run more than one gglearn process
not: shares counters across processes automatically

cards.subject: The gglearn README database warning
says: says SQLite is for development and to move to Postgres before multi-user production use
cards.use: are judging how far the current gglearn database setup scales

cards.subject: The deploy remote shell step
says: pipes remote steps into bash because the server login shell is fish
avoids fish failing on bash-only syntax
cards.use: wonder why remote deploy commands are piped into bash

qa.q: What does an architecture decision record capture?
qa.right: One significant decision, its context and its consequences
wrong: Every commit made to the codebase
The test results of the last release
The names of everyone on the team
qa.why: An ADR records why a significant choice was made so later readers can revisit it.

qa.q: What is the difference between latency and throughput?
qa.right: Latency is the time one request takes; throughput is how much work completes per unit of time
wrong: Latency is work completed per second; throughput is the time one request takes
Latency applies only to databases and throughput only to networks
They are two names for the same measurement
qa.why: They measure different things and can move independently.

qa.q: Which approach adds capacity by running more copies of a service behind a load balancer?
qa.right: Horizontal scaling
qa.why: Horizontal scaling adds instances; vertical scaling enlarges one machine.

qa.q: A service must be available 99.9% of the time over a 30-day month. Roughly how much downtime does that allow?
qa.right: About 43 minutes
qa.why: 0.1% of 43,200 minutes is about 43 minutes.

qa.q: Which HTTP method is both safe and idempotent?
qa.right: GET
qa.why: GET does not change state; PUT and DELETE are idempotent but not safe.

qa.q: Which C4 diagram shows the web app, API and database as separate boxes with their technologies?
qa.right: The container diagram
qa.why: Containers are the separately runnable parts of a system.

qa.q: Which caching pattern does this code show?
qa.right: Cache-aside
qa.why: The application checks the cache, loads from the database on a miss and fills the cache itself.

qa.q: What does an HTTP 429 response mean?
qa.right: The client has sent too many requests
wrong: The server is down for maintenance
The request took too long to arrive
The request body was too large
qa.why: 429 is the rate-limiting status; Retry-After may say when to try again.

qa.q: What problem does the random factor in this retry delay solve?
qa.right: Clients that failed together do not all retry at the same instant
wrong: It removes the need for a timeout
It guarantees the delay never exceeds the cap
qa.why: Jitter spreads retries so they do not arrive as a synchronized wave.

qa.q: Which is a real cost of moving from a monolith to microservices?
qa.right: Calls become network calls that can fail or be slow, so partial failure must be handled
wrong: Code can no longer be tested
Teams can no longer deploy independently
Data can no longer be stored in a database
qa.why: Distribution adds latency, partial failure and operational overhead.

qa.q: During a network partition, what does a CP system do?
qa.right: Rejects or delays some requests to keep data consistent
wrong: Accepts writes on both sides and merges them later
Silently serves stale data from every node
qa.why: CP systems give up availability for consistency during a partition.

qa.q: What does this statement do if another transaction already changed the row?
qa.right: It updates zero rows, so the caller knows there was a conflict
wrong: It overwrites the other change silently
It blocks until the other transaction commits
It always raises a deadlock error
qa.why: The version check in WHERE makes the write fail to match, which is optimistic locking.

qa.q: Which API style lets the client choose the exact fields returned from a single endpoint?
qa.right: GraphQL
wrong: REST with one URL per resource
qa.why: GraphQL queries name the fields wanted.

qa.q: Why does offset pagination misbehave on a feed with frequent inserts?
qa.right: Rows shift between requests, so items can repeat or be skipped
qa.why: Cursor pagination anchors to an item instead of a position.

qa.q: What does a circuit breaker do while it is open?
qa.right: Fails calls immediately without contacting the dependency
wrong: Sends all traffic to the database
qa.why: Open means calls are short-circuited until a probe suggests recovery.

qa.q: Why is rollback fast in a blue-green deployment?
qa.right: The previous environment is still running and traffic is switched back
wrong: The database is restored from backup automatically
qa.why: Keeping the old environment warm makes rollback a traffic switch.

qa.q: What does a feature flag separate?
qa.right: Deploying code from releasing the feature to users
qa.why: Flags let code ship dark and be enabled or disabled without a deploy.

qa.q: Three services each need to react to every order-placed event. Which fits best?
qa.right: Publish-subscribe, so each service receives its own copy
wrong: A single queue with three competing consumers
Each service guessing from the order count
qa.why: Competing consumers split messages; pub/sub copies them to every subscriber.

qa.q: What is the first question in a basic threat model?
qa.right: What are we building?
wrong: Who will be blamed for a breach?
qa.why: Threat modelling starts by understanding the system, then asking what can go wrong.

qa.q: A reporting service only reads orders, but its database account can drop tables. Which principle does this break?
qa.right: Least privilege
qa.why: The account holds more access than its task needs.

qa.q: A team of five with one product and no scaling problems wants to start with twelve microservices. What should you do first?
qa.right: Start with a modular monolith with clear module boundaries and split later if a real need appears
wrong: Build all twelve so the design is future-proof
Give every service the same shared database and call it micro
Skip boundaries because a monolith needs no structure
qa.why: Distribution has a cost; boundaries keep the option to split open.

qa.q: Users see old product prices for minutes after an update. Prices are cached with a 10 minute TTL. What is the most direct fix if prices must refresh quickly?
qa.right: Invalidate or update the cache entry when the price changes, keeping a short TTL as a backstop
wrong: Increase the TTL so fewer misses occur
qa.why: Event-driven invalidation bounds staleness; TTL alone does not.

qa.q: A new engineer asks why the team chose a document database two years ago and nobody remembers. What practice would have prevented this?
qa.right: Writing an architecture decision record
qa.why: ADRs preserve context and consequences next to the code.

qa.q: A service is slow under load but the load balancer keeps sending it traffic. What helps?
qa.right: Health checks that remove unhealthy instances from rotation
qa.why: Health checks let the balancer stop routing to failing instances.

qa.q: A one-day marketing event will cause a large spike, then traffic falls. Which approach fits cost best?
qa.right: Elastic scaling that adds capacity for the event and removes it afterwards
qa.why: Elasticity avoids paying for idle capacity.

qa.q: A payment API client times out and retries, and some customers were charged twice. What should the design add?
qa.right: An idempotency key so the server applies a repeated request only once
wrong: Sticky sessions on the load balancer
A switch from POST to GET
qa.why: The key lets the server recognise a retry of the same operation.

qa.q: An order service updates its database and then publishes an event, but a crash between the two sometimes loses the event. Which pattern fixes this?
qa.right: The transactional outbox
wrong: Publishing first and updating the database afterwards
Adding a retry around the publish only
qa.why: Writing the event in the same transaction makes the update and the event atomic.

qa.q: Checkout calls a recommendations service that has become slow and checkout threads are all waiting. What should you add first?
qa.right: A timeout and circuit breaker around the call, with a fallback such as showing no recommendations
qa.why: Fail fast and degrade gracefully so a non-critical dependency cannot block checkout.

qa.q: After a bad release you want the next one to expose problems to as few users as possible. Which approach fits?
qa.right: A canary release
wrong: A big-bang replacement during off hours
Deploying to everyone and watching the logs
Asking users to opt in to bug reports
qa.why: A canary limits the blast radius of a defect.

qa.q: Two services read and write the same tables and a column rename broke the other service. What is the underlying problem and fix?
qa.right: Shared-database integration; give each service ownership of its data and expose it through an API or events
wrong: Too few replicas; add read replicas
A wrong column type; use a larger type
qa.why: A shared schema is a hidden contract that couples services.

qa.q: Users in two regions edit the same shopping cart and the link between regions fails for a while. The business wants carts to always accept items. What should you choose?
qa.right: Favour availability with eventual consistency and merge carts when the link returns
wrong: Reject all cart updates until the regions reconnect
Use two-phase commit across regions for every add
Lock the cart in one region permanently
qa.why: Carts tolerate merging; blocking adds loses sales.

qa.q: Architecture rules forbid the UI layer calling the database, but violations keep appearing in pull requests. What fits evolutionary architecture?
qa.right: Add an automated fitness function to the build that fails on such dependencies
wrong: Review every pull request manually forever
qa.why: Automated checks keep an architectural rule from eroding.

qa.q: A mobile app and a web app need very different payloads from one backend, and the shared API grows many flags. What helps?
qa.right: A backend for frontend per client type
qa.why: A tailored API per client avoids one overloaded general API.

qa.q: A rate limiter behind a proxy is bypassed by attackers sending a forged X-Forwarded-For header. What is the right fix?
qa.right: Trust only the entries added by your own proxies, counting a fixed number of hops from the end of the header
wrong: Trust the first address in the header
Block every request carrying the header
qa.why: Each hop appends the address it saw, so only the tail is trustworthy.

qa.q: A deploy's schema push would drop a column holding data. How should a safe pipeline behave?
qa.right: Stop and fail so a person can plan a safe migration
wrong: Skip schema changes and continue the deploy
qa.why: Destructive changes need a deliberate, reviewed migration.

qa.q: Sessions live in each instance's memory and users are logged out as the load balancer moves them between three instances. What is the fix?
qa.right: Move session state to a shared store or use signed tokens so any instance can serve the user
qa.why: Horizontal scaling needs state outside the instance.

qa.q: A cache entry for a popular page expires and thousands of requests hit the database at once, which falls over. What mitigates this?
qa.right: Request coalescing so one request refreshes the entry, with staggered expiry
wrong: Shortening every TTL to one second
qa.why: A stampede is many simultaneous misses on one key.

qa.q: A sharded user table uses user id modulo shard count, and one celebrity account saturates its shard. What is the best next step?
qa.right: Treat the hot key specifically, for example by caching or splitting its load, because adding shards will not spread one key
qa.why: A single key always maps to one shard.

qa.q: A legacy monolith must be replaced over two years while features keep shipping. Which approach fits?
qa.right: The strangler fig pattern, routing slices of traffic to new code over time
wrong: Freezing features and rewriting in parallel before a cut-over
Rewriting the least important parts first and hiding it
Running two copies and letting users choose
qa.why: Incremental replacement keeps delivering value and limits risk.

qa.q: Teams are split by layer (frontend, backend, database) and every feature needs three teams. What does Conway's law suggest leaders consider?
qa.right: Reorganising into cross-functional teams aligned to the desired service boundaries
wrong: Merging services in code to match the teams
Nothing, since organisation does not affect architecture
qa.why: System structure follows communication structure, so shape the teams to get the design.

qa.q: Management wants 99.99% availability for an internal tool used only in office hours. What should the architect do first?
qa.right: Ask what an hour of downtime costs and derive the target from the business need
wrong: Accept the number and buy more servers
Promise it for the database only
qa.why: Targets should come from business impact; each nine adds cost.

qa.q: A saga spans payment, stock and shipping. Shipping fails after payment succeeded and stock was reserved. What should happen?
qa.right: Run compensating actions such as refunding the payment and releasing the stock
wrong: Issue a single database ROLLBACK across all three
qa.why: Sagas undo completed local steps with compensations.

qa.q: The only argument for adopting microservices is that a famous company uses them. What is the sound response?
qa.right: Evaluate team size, change rate, scaling needs and operational maturity, and record the decision with its trade-offs
wrong: Adopt them because they are proven at scale
Reject them because the company is larger
qa.why: Decisions should rest on your own constraints, written down so they can be revisited.

qa.q: A user posts a comment but does not see it on reload because reads go to a lagging replica. What is the lowest-cost fix?
qa.right: Route that user's reads to the primary for a short time after a write
wrong: Make every read use global consensus
qa.why: Read-your-writes can be provided selectively without giving up replicas.

qa.q: Two nodes both accept writes after a network split because each believes it is the leader. What would have prevented it?
qa.right: Requiring a quorum to elect and keep a leader
qa.why: Only the side holding a majority may act as leader.

qa.q: Which process manager runs the gglearn Next.js app in production?
qa.right: PM2
qa.why: The gglearn-web app is run by PM2 behind Apache and Cloudflare.

qa.q: What triggers a gglearn production deploy?
qa.right: A push to main runs a GitHub Actions workflow that calls the deploy script
wrong: A nightly cron job on the database
qa.why: The workflow runs the deploy script on every push to main.

qa.q: Why does the gglearn deploy script take a flock lock?
qa.right: So two deploys cannot run at the same time
wrong: To lock user accounts during a release
qa.why: The lock serialises deploys.

qa.q: Why does the live ggmoney server use MySQL?
qa.right: The machine already had MySQL 8 and a PHP driver, so no new server packages were needed
wrong: SQLite cannot be used from PHP
MySQL is faster at money arithmetic
qa.why: The choice followed what the server already had.

qa.q: Which files does the gglearn deploy keep out of the rsync so secrets and data never travel with code?
qa.right: node_modules, build output, databases and environment files
wrong: Nothing; the whole folder is copied
qa.why: Excluding databases and environment files protects data and secrets.

qa.q: Why are the remote deploy steps piped into bash?
qa.right: The server's login shell is fish, which cannot parse some bash syntax
qa.why: Piping into bash avoids fish syntax problems.

qa.q: gglearn's rate limiter keeps counters in process memory and the team plans to run four PM2 processes. What must change first?
qa.right: Move the counters to shared storage such as the database, since per-process counts would differ and reset on restart
wrong: Nothing, since the counters synchronise automatically
qa.why: In-memory counters are only valid while the app runs as a single process.

qa.q: Why does ggmoney keep a separate schema per database driver rather than translating at runtime?
qa.right: A silent translation bug in a finance app is worse than some duplication
wrong: It reduces the number of files
qa.why: Explicit schemas trade duplication for safety.

qa.q: What does the gglearn deploy do when a schema change would delete rows?
qa.right: It stops and fails because the drizzle-kit push is run without a force flag
wrong: It deletes the rows and continues
It forces the push after a delay
It skips the build and restarts PM2
qa.why: There is deliberately no force flag so destructive changes must be handled by a person.

qa.q: After deploying, how does the gglearn deploy script check the release?
qa.right: It requires the app to answer HTTP 200 several times and fails, showing PM2 error logs, if it does not
wrong: It only checks that PM2 reports online
It runs the full test suite on the server
It asks a person to open the site
qa.why: The check fails loudly and shows logs.

qa.q: Why is the gglearn-web app bound to 127.0.0.1 port 3400?
qa.right: So it is reachable only through Apache rather than directly from the internet
wrong: To let Cloudflare connect to it directly
qa.why: Binding to loopback keeps the app behind the reverse proxy.

qa.q: You must choose between strong consistency and availability for a stock-reservation counter that must never oversell. What do you choose and accept?
qa.right: Strong consistency, accepting higher latency or rejected requests during failures
wrong: No consistency model, using a cache
qa.why: Overselling is a correctness failure, so consistency wins over availability for this data.

qa.q: Which statement about the CAP theorem is correct?
qa.right: It forces the consistency versus availability choice only while a network partition is happening
wrong: It says a system can pick any two of the three at all times
It applies only to single-node databases
It says partitions never occur in the cloud
qa.why: Outside a partition a system can offer both, though PACELC notes the latency trade-off.
